responses.response: Use an internal Container_Api for your API and a System_External for the payment provider. Connect them with a calls relationship, labeled with the business action such as Creates payment, and put the technology on that relationship as HTTPS. Keep the provider as an external system instead of modeling it like one of your own containers unless you are intentionally decomposing the third-party side.

Apply the explicit queue pattern from the shared spec: model the publisher as a Container_Api, RabbitMQ as a Container_Queue, and the worker as a processing container such as Container_ProcessingServer. Use async relationships for the publish and consume legs, with technology AMQP. The mistake to avoid is drawing a direct calls relationship from the API to the worker, or otherwise bypassing the queue, because that makes the flow look synchronous and removes the decoupling.

Model Redis as a separate storage-style container, typically a Container_Database named clearly as Redis Cache with technology Redis, alongside the Postgres Container_Database. Show the API reading from the cache, and still show the API reading and writing Postgres as the source of truth; if useful, add a writes relationship from the API to Redis for cache warm-up or invalidation. Avoid showing only API -> Redis, or chaining API -> Redis -> Postgres, because that suggests Redis replaces or owns the primary data.

Model Stripe with two distinct interactions. First, your internal Container_Api calls the external Stripe system to create the payment over HTTPS. Second, model a separate async relationship from Stripe back to your internal webhook-receiving endpoint over HTTPS. If the webhook lands in the same API, it helps to show a dedicated internal component or endpoint for that receiver so the second leg is visibly separate. Avoid a reverse calls arrow that looks like the synchronous response to the create-payment request; the webhook is a later, independent event.
